title: The Role of the State
text: The Role of the State 4 Joskow, P. L. (2005), Regulation of Natural Monopolies, MIT CEEPR Working Paper 05-008, pages 8, 20–21, 93–94 and 119; Shleifer, A. (1998), State versus private ownership, Journal of Economic Perspectives 12(4), pages 8–9 of the NBER version. Problem Why it arises What the state does Natural monopoly One firm supplies the market at lower total cost than two Owns, franchises or regulates the supplier Sunk costs Assets cannot be moved, so the firm can be held up Gives legal protection and credible commitments Incomplete contracts Contracts cannot specify quality in full Chooses who owns, builds and operates Asymmetric information The firm knows its costs better than the regulator Audits, benchmarks and sets incentives

title: Natural Monopoly: Subadditive Costs
text: Natural Monopoly: Subadditive Costs 4 Definition: one firm supplies the market at lower total cost than two or more Scale economies: they are sufficient, not necessary: demand may be too small for two efficient firms Sunk costs: they explain why a single supplier survives, and why it can be held up after it invests The trade: a monopoly can be cheaper to run and costlier to use Joskow, P. L. (2005), Regulation of Natural Monopolies, MIT CEEPR Working Paper 05-008, pages 8–11 and 20–21. Cost function C(q) = F + cq as in Joskow, page 9; parameters illustrative.

title: Public Ownership, Franchising or Regulation
text: Public Ownership, Franchising or Regulation 4 Where cost cutting harms quality that cannot be written into a contract, public ownership can be the better arrangement (Shleifer, 1998, p. 11). Shleifer, A. (1998), State versus private ownership, Journal of Economic Perspectives 12(4), pages 8–11 of the NBER version; Joskow, P. L. (2005), MIT CEEPR Working Paper 05-008, pages 64–66 and 93–94. Response Idea Main weakness Public ownership The government owns and runs the supplier Weak incentives to cut cost and to innovate Franchise bidding Competition for the market replaces regulation Needs many independent bidders; the contract is incomplete Regulation A regulator sets prices that cover cost The regulator knows less than the firm

title: Data Centres and the Local Economy
text: Data Centres and the Local Economy 4 Method: an instrument built from nineteenth-century railway corridors and fibre access points Gains: employment, payroll and the number of firms rise in the host county Pressures: house prices, electricity prices and public water withdrawals rise as well, the last two later Wholesale: data centres raised US wholesale power prices by 6.9 per cent by 2025 and by 15.0 per cent in northern Virginia Alvarez, F. E., Argente, D., Chow, J. and Van Patten, D. (2026), NBER Working Paper 35194, pages 2 to 4; Kay, O., Reaser, R. and Taylor, R. (2026), Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper 2606, abstract.

title: National Totals and Local Constraints: Water and the Grid
text: National Totals and Local Constraints: Water and the Grid 4 Water: data centres use 5 million litres a day in England, a five-hundredth of what leaks lose Concentration: the six largest of 257 surveyed use 65 per cent of the sector's water Grid: applications from large users reached 125 GW against a peak demand of 58 GW, at least 80 GW from data centres Siting: water use per kilowatt-hour varies by place and hour, so location decides the effect Environment Agency (2024 to 2025); WRc and MOSL (2026), Water Efficient Data Centres; Ofgem figures as reported in the Spectator's Reality Check (August 2026); Li, P., Yang, J., Islam, M. A. and Ren, S. (2025), Making AI less thirsty, Communications of the ACM, DOI 10.1145/3724499.

title: Public Investment Management
text: Public Investment Management 4 Four stages: appraisal, selection, implementation and evaluation, scored from 0 to 4 for 71 countries Weak points: appraisal and evaluation score lowest in every region Spread: scores run from South Africa and Colombia at the top to Belize and Yemen at the bottom Income: Bolivia and Rwanda score above 2, ahead of 19 middle-income countries Dabla-Norris, E., Brumby, J., Kyobe, A., Mills, Z. and Papageorgiou, C. (2011), Investing in public investment: an index of public investment efficiency, IMF Working Paper 11/37, pages 14–17.

title: PIMA: Design Outruns Effectiveness
text: PIMA: Design Outruns Effectiveness 4 PIMA: scores 15 institutions across planning, allocation and implementation Design and practice: institutions are generally stronger on paper than in implementation Effectiveness: it is low at every stage and in every income group The gain: better governance could make up more than half of observed efficiency losses Verdier, G. (2020), Strong Infrastructure Governance for Strong Recovery, IMF Fiscal Affairs Department, slides 4 and 5 (CC0); Schwartz, G., Fouad, M., Hansen, T. and Verdier, G. (eds) (2020), Well Spent, IMF.

title: Cost-of-Service Regulation and Price Caps
text: Cost-of-Service Regulation and Price Caps 4 Revenue requirement = operating cost + depreciation + allowed return × regulatory asset base + other costs (Joskow, 2005, p. 98). Joskow, P. L. (2005), Regulation of Natural Monopolies, MIT CEEPR Working Paper 05-008, pages 94–99, 113–115, 119–128 and 146. Cost-of-service regulation Price cap or sliding scale How price is set Operating cost, depreciation and a return on the regulatory asset base, reset in a rate case A price path fixed in advance, partly responsive to realised cost What the firm keeps Savings until the next rate case Savings between reviews, shared by formula Main risk Too much capital, since the return is on the base Cost cutting that lowers quality; ratchet effects

title: Regulatory Design and Renegotiation
text: Regulatory Design and Renegotiation 4 Sample: more than 1,000 concessions in Latin America and the Caribbean, 1985 to 2000 A regulator: 17 per cent renegotiated where one existed, 61 where none did The regime: price caps 42 per cent, rate of return 13 The rules: 17 per cent when set in law, 28 in a decree and 40 in the contract Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute, Table 1.16 (page 17) and pages 12 and 16.

title: Capture, Ratchets and Hold-up
text: Capture, Ratchets and Hold-up 4 Joskow, P. L. (2005), Regulation of Natural Monopolies, MIT CEEPR Working Paper 05-008, pages 61, 93–99, 119–120, 126 and 146. Problem Mechanism Institutional response Information gap The firm knows its costs and effort better than the regulator Uniform accounts, audits, benchmarking Capture The firm or another group bends the regulator's decisions Transparency, appeals, legislative oversight Ratchet Savings revealed now are taken at the next review Regulatory lag; profit sharing Hold-up Sunk assets invite expropriation after investment Legal protection; credible commitment

title: Delivery Models and the PPP Framework
text: Delivery Models and the PPP Framework 4 The delivery spectrum: from management contracts to privatisation, and who bears which risk Bundling build and operate: Hart (2003): what the contract can specify decides the choice Sharing demand risk: Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013): a guarantee, a cap and a variable term The price of private finance: National Audit Office (2018): what the bundle must save The framework around the contract: Verhoest and co-authors (2015): government support across 20 countries

title: The Delivery Spectrum
text: The Delivery Spectrum 4 Between public supply and private supply lie outsourcing, leases, franchises, build-operate-transfer and divestiture. Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute, Table 2.1 (page 25) and Figure 2.1 (page 24). title: Hart (2003): Bundling Build and Operate
text: Hart (2003): Bundling Build and Operate 4 Question: should one firm build and run the asset, or should separate firms? Model: the builder makes two investments the contract cannot verify: a better building, and corner-cutting that lowers cost and quality Result: bundling gives the builder the operating saving, so he invests more in the building and cuts more corners Rule: conventional provision if the building can be specified and the service cannot; a PPP in the opposite case Hart, O. (2003), Incomplete contracts and public ownership: remarks, and an application to public-private partnerships, Economic Journal 113(486), C69–C76; CMPO Working Paper 03/061, pages 5–11.

title: Bundling and the Limits of the Contract
text: Bundling and the Limits of the Contract 4 Neither specified: the PPP beats conventional provision, 1.5 against 0, because the builder invests more Service specified: the PPP rises to 3 as corner-cutting is penalised Building specified: conventional provision reaches the first best, 4 Author's calculation from Hart's (2003) model, with functional forms chosen by the author (models_w2.py); psi = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 2, delta = 1.5. CMPO Working Paper 03/061, pages 6–10.

title: Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013): Sharing Demand Risk
text: Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013): Sharing Demand Risk 4 Setting: a risk-averse firm builds and runs a project whose demand is uncertain, and subsidies waste more than user fees First result: PPPs do not release public funds: the saving now is given back as fees forgone later Optimal contract: a minimum revenue guarantee, a revenue cap and a variable term In practice: observed guarantees and revenue-sharing clauses bear no relation to the optimum Engel, E., Fischer, R. and Galetovic, A. (2013), The basic public finance of public-private partnerships, Journal of the European Economic Association 11(1), 83–111; NBER Working Paper 13284, pages 2–6, 12–16 and 41.

title: The Optimal Concession Contract
text: The Optimal Concession Contract 4 Low demand: the concession runs on and the state tops up to the guarantee Intermediate: the firm keeps what it collects, and no subsidy is paid High demand: the concession ends at the cap, and the state takes the excess Author's calculation from the model of Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013), NBER Working Paper 13284, pages 12–16, with exponential utility and uniform demand chosen by the author; I = 100, demand 70–170, risk aversion 0.01, zeta = 0.25, lambda = 0.3.

title: Private Finance and the Public Sector Comparator
text: Private Finance and the Public Sector Comparator 4 The premium: 2 to 3.75 points over gilts in the 2010 plan, 2 to 4 for deals since 2013, and over 8 per cent in four 2013 housing deals Compounding: £100 over 30 years costs £34 in interest at 2 per cent and £73 at 4 Comparators: PF2 schools cost about 40 per cent more than government borrowing, a privately financed hospital 70 per cent more The offset: no evidence of operational efficiency in the NAO's hospital samples National Audit Office (2018), PFI and PF2, HC 718, paragraphs 1.9 and 1.17–1.19 and Figures 3 and 4 (pages 10 and 14–16); bars computed by the author from the annuity formula, which reproduces Figure 3.

title: The Saving Needed to Offset Private Finance
text: The Saving Needed to Offset Private Finance 4 Gilts plus 2.0: the bundle must cut operating cost by 38 per cent Gilts plus 3.75: 72 per cent Gilts plus 5.5: more than all of it, 108 per cent Author's calculation after National Audit Office (2018), PFI and PF2, paragraphs 1.17–1.19, 30 years, gilts 2.5%, operating cost 4% of capital a year (author's assumption), fee 1%, company costs 1.5%.

title: PPP Frameworks across Europe
text: PPP Frameworks across Europe 4 Index: policy commitment, legal framework and supporting arrangements in 20 countries, each scored from 1 to 4 Range: the United Kingdom scores 3.0, the highest, and Estonia 1.2, the lowest No package: the UK, the Netherlands and Germany score high on policy and low on PPP law Uptake: a correlation of 0.31 with the value of PPPs relative to GDP, and 0.58 with the number of projects Verhoest, K., Petersen, O. H., Scherrer, W. and Soecipto, R. M. (2015), Transport Reviews 35(2), 118–139; Murwantara, R. (2023), doctoral thesis, University of Antwerp, chapter 2, Table 3 (page 30) and page 34.

title: Three Models of the Contract Compared
text: Three Models of the Contract Compared 4 Hart (2003), pages 5–11; Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013), pages 2–6 and 15; National Audit Office (2018), paragraphs 1.9 and 1.17–1.19; Verhoest et al. (2015) as reported in Murwantara (2023), chapter 2, page 34. Model Explains Prediction Evidence Hart (2003) Whether to bundle build and operate Bundle if the service can be specified and the building cannot Model only; sector examples Engel et al. (2013) How to share demand risk A guarantee and a cap; no budget relief Renegotiation follows low demand National Audit Office (2018) What the bundle must save The finance premium has to be earned back Premium of 2–4 points; thin evidence of savings Verhoest et al. (2015) What governments do to support PPPs Support varies and is not a package Weak link to uptake, r = 0.31

title: Development Finance Institutions
text: Development Finance Institutions 4 Role: multilateral banks lend directly, and are expected to mobilise private lenders Signalling: lending on commercial terms signals opportunity and can encourage reform Risk mitigation: preferred creditor status, close monitoring and information reduce political risk for private lenders Scale: an annual investment gap of about USD 2.5 trillion against aid of USD 143 billion in 2016 Broccolini, C., Lotti, G., Maffioli, A., Presbitero, A. and Stucchi, R. (2019), Mobilization Effects of Multilateral Development Banks, IDB Invest Technical Note 16, pages 1 and 14.

title: Mobilisation Effects of Multilateral Lenders
text: Mobilisation Effects of Multilateral Lenders 4 Data: syndicated loans to developing countries, 1993 to 2017 Finding: a multilateral lender present for three years raises the number of loans, their size, the banks per loan and their maturity Robustness: no decline in bond finance and no sign of anticipation Caution: the effect on the number of loans is significant only at 10 per cent Broccolini, C., Lotti, G., Maffioli, A., Presbitero, A. and Stucchi, R. (2019), Mobilization Effects of Multilateral Development Banks, IDB Invest Technical Note 16, Table 3 (page 30).

title: Concessions and Renegotiation
text: Concessions and Renegotiation 4 Frequency: 30 per cent of more than 1,000 concessions were renegotiated, and 41.5 per cent excluding telecoms Sectors: water 74 per cent, transport 55, electricity 10 Timing: on average 2.2 years after award, and 85 per cent within four years Outcome: on average, users were worse off Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute, Tables 1.7 to 1.9 (pages 13–14) and page 12.

title: Contract Features and Renegotiation
text: Contract Features and Renegotiation 4 Award criterion: 60 per cent renegotiated when awarded on the lowest tariff, 11 on the highest transfer fee Obligations: 70 per cent with investment requirements, 18 with performance indicators Process: 46 per cent when bid competitively, 8 when negotiated bilaterally Reading: competition for the market buys a low price and a contract that is later reopened Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute, Table 1.16 (page 17) and Table 1.11 (page 15).

title: Initiators of Renegotiation
text: Initiators of Renegotiation 4 Who asks: operators requested 61 per cent of renegotiations and governments 26 Price caps: operators initiated 83 per cent of renegotiations Rate of return: governments initiated 34 per cent, and operators 26 Design: a guarantee and cap agreed in advance replace a negotiation after demand falls short Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute, Tables 1.13 and 1.14 (page 16); Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013), page 2.
